results.title: Authenticate to Sherlock AI with API keys on CloudFerro Cloud 
excerpts:
# Authenticate to Sherlock AI with API keys on CloudFerro Cloud 

Sherlock AI uses API keys to authenticate programmatic requests to AI models. You create API keys inside a Sherlock AI project in the control panel and then use them from your application, automation script, or backend service.

Treat every API key as a secret. Do not share it with other users, commit it to a repository, paste it into documentation, or expose it in client-side code such as browsers and mobile applications. Production requests should go through your own backend, where the key can be loaded from an environment variable or a secrets management service.

## Prerequisites 

Before you start, make sure that:

1. You can log in to the Sherlock AI control panel after completing [account and organization setup](docs.cloudferro.com/en/latest/sherlock/How-to-set-up-Sherlock-AI-on-CloudFerro-Cloud/How-to-set-up-Sherlock-AI-on-CloudFerro-Cloud.html).
2. You have [selected the project](docs.cloudferro.com/en/latest/sherlock/Manage-Sherlock-projects-on-CloudFerro-Cloud/Manage-Sherlock-projects-on-CloudFerro-Cloud.html) where the API key will be created.
3. Your account has permissions to manage API keys in that project.
4. You know where the key will be stored after creation, because Sherlock AI shows the generated key only once.

## Step 1: Open API Keys 

Log in to the Sherlock AI control panel and open the project in which you want to create the key. In the left navigation menu, select **API Keys** under **Resources**. The current console uses **Create API Key** for the creation action. The screenshots below show the earlier console layout, where this action is called **Add API key**.

The API keys page lists the keys already created in the current project. Use this page to check existing keys, create a new one, and manage project-level authentication for programmatic access.

[image: Sherlock AI API Keys page]

*API Keys page in the Sherlock AI control panel. [](#id1)*

## Step 2: Start creating a new key 

Click **Create API Key** (**Add API key** in the earlier interface) to open the key creation window. Enter a clear name for the key, for example the name of the application, service, environment, or automation workflow that will use it.

A descriptive name is important later, especially when several keys exist in the same project. It helps you recognize which application uses which key and makes key rotation safer.

[image: Create API Keys window]

*Window for entering the API key name before generation. [](#id2)*

## Step 3: Generate and copy the key 

After entering the name, generate the key. Sherlock AI displays the new API key immediately after creation.

Copy the key at this stage and store it in a secure location. This is the only time the full key is shown. If you close the window before saving it, you will need to create another key.

[image: Newly generated Sherlock AI API key]

*Newly generated API key. Copy it before closing the window. [](#id3)*

## Step 4: Verify that the key was created 

After copying the key, return to the API keys page and verify that the new entry is visible in the list. The list shows the key name and creation date, which helps you identify recently created keys and distinguish them from older credentials.

Keep only the keys that are still needed. When a key is no longer used, replace it in your application first, verify that the new key works, and then remove the old one from the project.

[image: List of Sherlock AI API keys]

*API keys list after a new key has been created. [](#id4)*

Home > > Get started with the Sherlock API on CloudFerro Cloud

Get started with the Sherlock API on CloudFerro Cloud 

An application needs an API key, a model identifier, and an endpoint before it can request an answer. Sherlock provides an OpenAI-compatible API for language, vision, and embedding models. You can use curl for a first terminal request or the OpenAI Python client for an application running on your computer or a virtual machine.
The procedure below prepares the client, lists available model IDs, and sends a first chat request. The same account and project used in My Portal provide the context for the API key.

Prerequisites 

No. 1 Access to a Sherlock project
Complete account and organization setup through My Portal, then create or select a project. Creating a project requires administrator privileges in the organization; for an existing project, use the access granted to your account.
No. 2 An API key for that project
Follow Authenticate with API keys to create and securely store a key. Your account needs permission to manage API keys in the selected project. Have the key available for the environment-variable setup below.
Warning
Keep the API key secret. Do not share it, commit it to a repository, or expose it in browser or mobile application code. Production requests must pass through your backend, where the key is loaded from an environment variable or a secret store.
No.

...

For Python requests, create and activate a virtual environment, then install the client. Skip this step if you only want to use curl.
On Linux or macOS:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install openai
On Windows PowerShell:
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install openai

Configure the API key 

Store the key in SHERLOCK_API_KEY in the terminal where you will run the examples. The following prompts accept the key without putting its value in the command you type or displaying it on screen.
In Bash on Linux or macOS:
read -r -s -p "Sherlock API key: " SHERLOCK_API_KEY
printf '\n'
export SHERLOCK_API_KEY
In Windows PowerShell:
$sherlockKey = Read-Host "Sherlock API key" -AsSecureString
$env:SHERLOCK_API_KEY = [System.Net.NetworkCredential]::new([string]::Empty, $sherlockKey).Password
Remove-Variable sherlockKey
The variable is available to programs launched from that terminal. Set it again in a new session, or configure it through your deployment’s secret storage. The Python examples explicitly read SHERLOCK_API_KEY and set base_url to the Sherlock service.

List available models 

Use either example to query GET /models before choosing the model for a request.

With curl 

curl api-sherlock.cloudferro.com/openai/v1/models \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $SHERLOCK_API_KEY"

With Python 

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["SHERLOCK_API_KEY"],
    base_url="api-sherlock.cloudferro.com/openai/v1",
)

models = client.models.list()
for model in models.data:
    print(model.id)
The Python example prints the model IDs; use print(models) to inspect the full response. The chat examples below use speakleash/Bielik-11B-v3.0-Instruct. If it is absent from your response, replace it with an available chat model ID. An embedding model is not a substitute for a chat model.

Send a request with curl 

Send a prompt to the chat completion endpoint. The command loads the API key from the environment and passes it as a bearer token.
curl api-sherlock.cloudferro.com/openai/v1/chat/completions \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $SHERLOCK_API_KEY" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
    "model": "speakleash/Bielik-11B-v3.0-Instruct",
    "messages": [
      {
        "role": "system",
        "content": "You are a helpful assistant."
      },
      {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Explain what Sherlock AI is in one paragraph."
      }
    ]
  }'
A successful request returns JSON containing the generated answer and response metadata.

Send a request with Python 

The client sends the same prompt to Sherlock and prints the generated answer.
import os
from openai import OpenAI

results.title: toolkit/gitbook/tools/sherlock/README.md at main · bellingcat/toolkit · GitHub
excerpts:
Sherlock is designed to be straightforward for open source investigations: it does not require API keys or login credentials for the sites it checks; instead, it simply constructs the expected profile URL for each site and observes the response to determine whether the username exists on a given platform. This means it only accesses publicly available information and cannot bypass privacy settings or account restrictions.

Sherlock is primarily a CLI tool, so some familiarity with the command line is required to install and run it. However, installation is relatively accessible: the latest version is published on PyPI for one-command install (e.g. `pipx install sherlock-project` or `pip install --user sherlock-project`).

...

### CLI Usage

```
# Single username (saves a user123.txt by default)
sherlock user123

# Multiple usernames
sherlock alice bob charlie

# Try common separators between name parts with the {?} helper
# (expands to _  -  . between tokens)
sherlock john{?}doe
```

...

## Requirements

* **Python 3.9+ environment** – Sherlock [requires Python 3.9](pypi.org/project/sherlock-project/) or higher installed on the system. Earlier versions are no longer supported in the latest release. Alternatively, Docker can be used to run Sherlock in a container, eliminating the need to install Python.
* **Internet connection** – An active internet connection is required since Sherlock needs to send HTTP requests to each target website to check for the username’s profile. The speed of results depends on network speed and the number of sites checked.
* **No account/API keys needed** – Sherlock uses direct web requests and does not require creating any account or API key to use. All searches are against publicly accessible URLs. (Be mindful of each site’s terms of service; Sherlock generates web traffic that in some cases might be seen as automated scraping).

...

* **Incomplete site coverage:** The tool focuses on global and popular services, but cannot cover every regional or niche platform. Investigators targeting local or emerging sites may need to supplement Sherlock with other tools, such as [_WhatsMyName_](whatsmyname.io/)_,_ or manual searching.
* **No profile analysis:** Sherlock only reports where a username appears. It does not cross-reference or analyse the profile content. Determining whether matching usernames across platforms belong to the same person is left to the investigator.
* **Outdated API:** There is no official Sherlock API. An experimental REST API exists but has not been maintained since 2021 and using it requires local setup. As of 2026, running Sherlock locally or via community web interfaces remains the recommended method.

excerpts:
sherlock-api 0.1.0

Python client for the Sherlock REST API
pip install sherlock-api Copy PIP instructions
* Description
* Metadata
* Release files
* Release history

sherlock-api 

Python client for the Sherlock REST API. Build your own Sherlock applications — create cases and batches, upload inspection images with measurements, write log entries, and drive modal dialogs and notifications in a running Sherlock process.

Install 

pip install sherlock-api
Requires Python 3.10+.

Quickstart 

from PIL import Image 
 from sherlock_api import ( 
    SherlockAPIClient , 
    CreateCaseRequest , 
    CreateBatchRequest , 
    RobotPlatform , 
    DecisionClass , 
 ) 

 with SherlockAPIClient ( sherlock_port = 8080 ) as client : 
    case = client . post_case ( 
        CreateCaseRequest ( 
            "Bushing inspection" , 
            RobotPlatform . UNIVERSAL_ROBOTS , 
            "0A0E012F7772596B03D92AAA544763BB" , 
        ) 
    ) 
    batch = client . post_batch ( CreateBatchRequest ( case [ "id" ], "Batch 1" )) 

    image , measurements = client . upload_image_with_measurements ( 
        Image . open ( "part.png" ), 
        "part.png" , 
        DecisionClass . Ok , 
        [( "diameter_mm" , 12.04 ), ( "roundness" , 0.98 )], 
        batch [ "id" ], 
    ) 

    client . log_batch_info ( batch [ "id" ], f "Uploaded { image [ 'image_name' ] } " )

Configuration 

Every constructor argument falls back to an environment variable. A script launched by Sherlock gets these for free, so SherlockAPIClient() with no arguments is usually all you need:
* Argument | Environment variable | Default
* sherlock_url | SHERLOCK_URL | localhost
* sherlock_port | SHERLOCK_PORT | — (required)
* sherlock_process_id | SHERLOCK_PROCESS_ID | None
* sherlock_case_id | SHERLOCK_CASE_ID | None
* sherlock_batch_id | SHERLOCK_BATCH_ID | None
The three id defaults are used whenever you omit the corresponding argument — client.get_case() reads sherlock_case_id , client.get_batch() reads sherlock_batch_id , and the process methods read sherlock_process_id . Omitting an argument that has no default raises SherlockConfigurationError .
Keyword-only options: request_timeout (seconds, default 30.0 ), max_retries (default 3 , applied to connection errors and 502/503/504 on GET and DELETE), and session to supply your own requests.Session .

Modal dialogs

...

Notifications 

from sherlock_api import CreateNotificationRequest , NotificationAttachment 

 client . post_notification ( 
    CreateNotificationRequest ( 
        "Batch finished" , 
        "42 parts inspected, 3 rejected." , 
        [ NotificationAttachment ( "report.pdf" , "application/pdf" , pdf_bytes )], 
    ) 
 )
A notification sent to a process that no longer exists is logged as a warning on the sherlock_api.client logger rather than raised — it is fire-and-forget.

API surface 

* Area | Methods
* Files | get_file , post_file , post_file_from_memory
* Cases | get_cases , get_case , post_case
* Batches | get_batch , get_batches_for_case , post_batch
* Images | get_image , get_images_for_batch , post_image , upload_image , upload_image_with_measurement , upload_image_with_measurements
* Logs | get_log , post_log , log_{case,batch,image}_{error,warning,info}
* Measurements | get_measurement , post_measurement , delete_measurement
* Processes | get_process_state , is_process_running , get_env_state , get_env_vars , post_modal , get_modal , delete_modal , post_notification
Methods returning JSON return the parsed dict or list from the server as-is.

Errors 

SherlockError
├── SherlockConfigurationError   (also a ValueError)  missing port or id
└── SherlockAPIError             (also a RuntimeError) unexpected HTTP status
    ├── SherlockBadRequestError  400
    ├── SherlockNotFoundError    404
    ├── SherlockTimeoutError     408
    └── SherlockServerError      5xx
SherlockAPIError carries .status_code , .reason , .body (truncated to 500 characters), .method and .url .
from sherlock_api import SherlockNotFoundError

## Configure MCP server with Sherlock

Add the configuration above to your project's

```
.mcp.json
```

file for Claude Code, then run

```
/mcp
```

in Claude Code to sign in to Apify. It connects to the hosted Apify MCP server with the Sherlock Actor already loaded. Clients without OAuth support can authenticate with an

```
Authorization: Bearer
```

header carrying an API token from API & Integrations in Apify Console.

For other MCP clients, get a client-specific configuration with the Sherlock Actor preconfigured at https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,misceres/sherlock.

You can connect to the Apify MCP server using an MCP client that supports Streamable HTTP.

If you want to learn more about our Apify MCP implementation, check out our MCP documentation. To learn more about the Model Context Protocol in general, refer to the official MCP documentation or read our blog post.
